title: The Great Outdoors
description: Ten calm stories and short texts about time outside: a hike in the Rocky Mountains, a first surfing lesson, camping by a river, a climbing gym, a kayak trip, a sunrise on a mountain and more.

lessons.title: Thin Air in the Rockies
lessons.summary: Hannah from Florida undertakes her first long hike in the Rocky Mountains and learns how hard it is to breathe up high.
lessons.text:
Hannah had always lived by the sea in Florida, where the highest point in her town was a bridge. So when her cousin Ben invited her to Colorado for a week, she decided to undertake something completely new: a full day's hike in the Rocky Mountains.

Ben, who had grown up in Denver, gave her some advice the evening before. "The trail starts at 9,000 feet," he said. "Up there, the air has less oxygen than you are used to. Your lungs will have to work harder, so walk slowly and breathe deeply. And drink plenty of fluids, even when you are not thirsty."

Hannah laughed. "It's only a walk. People undertake much harder things than that every day."

The next morning they set off early. For the first hour, the path climbed gently through tall pines, and the cool air smelled of wood and wet earth. Then the trees grew shorter and the path grew steeper. Soon Hannah could hear her own heart. Each breath felt thin, as if someone had taken half of the oxygen out of the air. She stopped, put her hands on her knees and tried to breathe slowly.

Ben waited beside her without saying a word. When she was ready, he handed her a bottle of water. "Fluids first," he said. "Small sips. Your body loses water quickly up here, because the air is so dry."

He was right about the dry air. By noon, Hannah's lips were cracked and sore, and she was grateful when Ben gave her a small tube of cream for her lips.

Above the trees, the mountains opened up around them. A wide meadow lay in front of them, and it was a riot of color: yellow, blue and deep red flowers covered the grass all the way to the gray rocks. Hannah had never seen such a riot of color, not even in a garden.

At the highest point of the trail, at about 12,000 feet, she felt a slight headache. Ben offered her a pill from his first aid kit, but she wanted to rest first. They sat on a flat rock, ate their sandwiches and looked down at the valley. After twenty minutes the headache was gone, and she did not need the pill after all.

On the way down, every step was easier. Her lungs seemed to fill without any effort, and she talked and laughed the whole way. "Next summer," she told Ben, "I want to undertake a longer hike. But I will bring my own cream for my lips."

Questions:
Why was the hike difficult for Hannah?
It was difficult because the air in the mountains has less oxygen, so her lungs had to work harder.
What advice did Ben give her?
He told her to walk slowly, breathe deeply and drink plenty of fluids.
What happened to Hannah's lips, and why?
Her lips became cracked and sore because the air was so dry.
What did the meadow look like?
It was a riot of color, with yellow, blue and red flowers.
Why did Hannah not take the pill?
She rested first, and after twenty minutes her headache was gone.
What does Hannah want to do next summer?
She wants to undertake a longer hike.

lessons.title: My First Surfing Lesson
lessons.summary: Rachel finally takes a surfing lesson at a small school by the beach and stands on a wave for three seconds.
lessons.text:
For years I had watched people surf on television and thought that it looked like flying. Last summer, at 34, I finally signed up for a first lesson at a small surf school in San Diego.

The school was a wooden shed at the end of the beach, painted bright blue. Above the door hung a sign with the school's logo: a white wave inside a yellow sun. The same logo was printed on every board and on the shirt of every teacher.

Registration took place at a table in front of the shed. A young woman named Kai found my name, Rachel Moore, on her list, asked me to sign a form and handed me a thick black suit for the cold water. Registration took five minutes, and soon I was standing on the sand with four other pupils.

Our teacher was a calm man with long gray hair named Luis. He told us that in winter he taught at an elementary school, and that teaching adults was not so different from teaching seven-year-olds. "Elementary rules first," he said with a smile. "Rule number one: always listen to your teacher."

For half an hour we practiced on the sand, lying on our boards and jumping up to our feet. Then Luis led his pupils into the water.

The ocean was colder than I had expected. Each wave threw a fine, salty spray into my face, and above us white birds were screaming as they circled over the water. Before we went any farther, a woman in our group asked the question that all of us were thinking: "What about sharks?"

Luis did not laugh at her. "Sharks live in this ocean, of course," he said. "But they almost never come into shallow water like this. I have taught here for 15 years, and I have never seen a shark near this beach." His calm voice made the sharks seem very far away.

My first five waves were not a success. Each time I tried to stand, the board slid away and I fell into the cold spray. On my sixth wave, however, I felt the board lift under me. I pushed myself up, bent my knees, and for three wonderful seconds I was standing. Then I heard myself screaming with joy.

After the lesson, Kai told us that the lessons were free for children from the neighborhood, thanks to a local sponsor. The sponsor, a family bakery, paid for their boards and teachers, and its logo was painted on the side of the shed. On my way home, I bought some bread from that bakery. It seemed the least I could do for a good sponsor.

Questions:
Where was the surf school?
It was in a blue wooden shed at the end of the beach.
What was the school's logo?
The logo was a white wave inside a yellow sun.
What did Luis do in winter?
He taught at an elementary school.
What did one woman ask before the pupils went farther into the water?
She asked about sharks.
What happened on Rachel's sixth wave?
She stood on the board for three seconds and heard herself screaming with joy.
Who paid for the children's lessons?
A family bakery paid for them as a local sponsor.

lessons.title: A Night by the River
lessons.summary: Tom and Grace camp by a slow river, cook a simple dinner and meet a musician who is writing a song.
lessons.text:
Tom and Grace arrived at a camping area by the Green River late on a Friday afternoon. Their site was just twelve steps from the water, on a patch of soft grass under two old trees. The river was wide and slow there, and the evening light turned its surface the color of honey.

Near the entrance, a sign listed the rules: fires were allowed only inside the metal rings, quiet hours began at ten, and nobody could cut branches from living trees. "We don't want to violate any rules on our first night," said Grace. So, instead of looking for wood in the forest, Tom bought a pile of dry wood at the gate and carried it to their site.

Dinner was simple: pasta with a tomato sauce that Grace had made at home and brought in a glass jar. She heated the sauce in a small pot over the fire while Tom boiled the pasta. Perhaps it was the fresh air, but the meal tasted delicious. "This is the most delicious sauce you have ever made," Tom said. Grace answered, smiling, that it was the same sauce as always.

For dessert, they toasted bread over the fire and spread it with strawberry jam. A jar of jam, they agreed, is one of the best things to bring on a camping trip.

As the sky grew dark, soft music came from the next site. A woman with short gray hair was playing the guitar and singing quietly. Later she walked over and introduced herself. Her name was Olivia, and she was a musician from Utah. She explained that she was really a piano teacher, but a piano is hard to take on a camping trip, so on trips she always brought her guitar instead.

Olivia was writing a song about the river, she said, and she still needed the lyrics for the last part. She asked Tom and Grace what they could hear. Grace listened for a moment and named what she heard: the water over the stones, the fire and an owl somewhere in the trees. Olivia wrote a few words in her notebook. "Good lyrics often come from simple things," she said. "Musicians just have to listen."

At ten o'clock exactly, Olivia put her guitar away. "I'm not going to violate quiet hours," she said, and walked back to her own site. Tom took one last piece from the pile of wood and added it to the fire. He and Grace sat and watched the stars until the flames were low.

Questions:
How far was their site from the water?
It was just twelve steps from the water.
Why did Tom buy a pile of wood at the gate?
He bought it because nobody could cut branches from living trees, and they did not want to violate any rules.
What did Tom and Grace eat for dinner?
They ate pasta with a tomato sauce that Grace had made at home.
What did they have for dessert?
They had toasted bread with strawberry jam.
Why did Olivia bring a guitar instead of a piano?
She brought a guitar because a piano is hard to take on a camping trip.
What did Olivia still need for her song?
She still needed the lyrics for the last part.

lessons.title: From Shopping Mall to Climbing Gym
lessons.summary: A short report on how an empty shopping mall became a large climbing gym.
lessons.text:
When the old mall in Oakwood closed its doors in 2019, many people in town expected the empty building to become a parking lot. Instead, this spring it opened again as one of the largest climbing gyms in the state. The transformation took three years, and the result is worth a visit.

The idea came from two friends, Sam Ortiz and Jenny Chen, who have climbed together since college. They looked at old factories first, but an empty mall had one great advantage: its central hall was 60 feet high. "Most people look at an old mall and see the past," Jenny said. "We saw 60 feet of open space." However, it is not simple to convert a mall into a gym, and many experts told them that it would cost too much to convert such a building.

First, the friends hired a contractor who had built sports halls before. The contractor and his team removed the shop fronts and the old food court. Then came the hardest part: a steel framework to hold the climbing walls. The walls are heavy, and hundreds of people hang from them every day, so the framework had to be far stronger than anything the mall had needed. Some of the original steel beams were strong enough to keep. Others were replaced with new beams, which the contractor brought in on trucks.

Every step of the work depended on careful measurement. Each wall has its own dimensions: some are wide and gentle, while others are narrow and lean out over the floor like a wave. The team checked every measurement twice, because a small error in the dimensions of one panel could leave a gap between two walls.

Before the gym could open, a city inspector visited the building four times. The inspector tested the beams, the floors and the thick mats under the walls, and she made sure that people could leave the building quickly in an emergency. On her last visit, she signed the papers, and the gym opened two weeks later.

Today, little of the old mall remains. The glass roof still lets in the light, and one old shop sign hangs above the coffee bar. Children who once came here with their parents to buy shoes now come back to climb. For many people in Oakwood, that is the best part of the transformation. Sam and Jenny did not just convert a building; they gave a dying place a new life.

Questions:
What did many people expect to happen to the empty mall?
They expected it to become a parking lot.
Why did Sam and Jenny choose the mall?
They chose it because its central hall was 60 feet high.
Why did the framework have to be so strong?
It had to be strong because the walls are heavy and hundreds of people hang from them every day.
Why did the team check every measurement twice?
A small error in the dimensions of one panel could leave a gap between two walls.
What did the inspector check?
She tested the beams, the floors and the mats, and she made sure that people could leave quickly in an emergency.
What is the best part of the transformation for many people?
A dying place has found a new life.

lessons.title: Priya Tries Climbing
lessons.summary: Priya visits a climbing gym for the first time with her friend Jordan and learns to use her feet.
lessons.text:
Priya had walked past the climbing gym on Hayes Street a hundred times before she finally went inside. Her friend Jordan, who climbed there often, had offered to show her the basics.

At the front desk, a young man named Marco spoke to them in a polite, formal way. "Good evening. Is this your first visit? Then I will need you to read and sign this form, and you will have to take a short safety class before you climb."

"Relax, Marco, she's with me," said Jordan.

Marco smiled, but he did not change the rules. "I'm sorry, but by default, every new member starts with the class."

During the twenty-minute safety class, Marco explained the gym's most important rule: no more than four people on a wall at the same time. "Please never exceed four," he said, "because climbers can fall on each other." Afterward, Priya rented a pair of climbing shoes. She had arrived in her old tennis shoes, but Marco told her that tennis shoes were too soft and wide for the small holds on the walls.

The people in the gym were truly diverse: a family with small children, two women of about 70, an older man and a group of college students. Priya liked that diverse crowd at once.

Jordan led her to the easiest wall. "Climbing is mostly about your feet," he said. "Don't try to pull yourself up with your arms. Keep a light grip and push with your legs."

Priya started up. Her grip was far too tight, and soon her fingers hurt. "A tight grip is a common weakness," Jordan said. "Everyone has that weakness at the beginning. Relax your hands."

On her second try, she reached for a big blue hold that belonged to a different route. "Did I just cheat?" she asked.

"A little," Jordan said, laughing. "But in here, you only cheat yourself."

Next to them, a girl of about ten was moving up the hardest wall very fast. "She's a little speed demon," Jordan said. The girl reached the top and came down smiling. Priya was impressed, and she told the girl so. "You're a demon on that wall," she said, and the girl looked very proud.

By the end of the evening, Priya had reached the top of the easiest wall three times. Her arms were shaking, but she was impressed with herself, too. At the desk, she asked Marco about a monthly pass.

"Certainly," he said, and then he smiled. "See you on Thursday?"

Questions:
Why did Priya have to take a safety class?
By default, every new member starts with a safety class.
How many people may be on a wall at the same time?
Climbers should never exceed four people on one wall.
Why could Priya not climb in her tennis shoes?
Tennis shoes are too soft and wide for the small holds on the walls.
What was Priya's weakness at the beginning?
A tight grip was her weakness, because she held on too hard.
Why did Priya ask if she had cheated?
She asked because she used a hold that belonged to a different route.
Why was Priya impressed by the girl?
She was impressed because the girl climbed the hardest wall very fast.

lessons.title: A River Day with My Teenager
lessons.summary: A father takes his 15-year-old son on a kayak trip, and they find a cave full of birds.
lessons.text:
My son Eli is 15, and like many teenagers, he would spend a whole Saturday in his room, playing multiplayer games with friends from three different countries. I don't think those games are bad. Still, last month I asked him to give me one Saturday without a screen, and to my surprise, he agreed.

We drove to a place that rents boats on a river in central Pennsylvania. On the way, I told Eli that Pennsylvania is not officially a state but a commonwealth, like Virginia, Kentucky and Massachusetts. He looked at me for a long moment. "Uh, okay," he said. "Is that going to be on a test?" I had to admit that the difference between a state and a commonwealth is mostly in the name.

There, a friendly man gave us two kayaks, two paddles and two orange life jackets. For the first ten minutes, Eli's boat turned in slow circles. "This is torture," he said, half laughing and half serious. "My arms are going to fall off."

I showed him how to pull the paddle back along the side of the boat. Soon he was moving in a straight line, and the torture, as he called it, was forgotten.

The river was calm and clear, and in places it was so shallow that we could see the stones on the bottom. About two miles down the river, the bank rose into a wall of gray rock, and at its foot there was a low, dark cave. We paddled closer and stopped. Hundreds of small birds were flying in and out of the cave. They were swallows, and the friendly man had told us that a colony of them came back to the cave every summer. The whole colony seemed to be talking at once.

Eli watched the birds for a long time without speaking. Then he said, "No offense, Dad, but this is actually better than I expected."

I told him that I did not take offense. In fact, coming from a teenager, it was close to the highest praise a parent can receive.

"It wasn't an insult," he said quickly.

"I know it wasn't an insult," I said. "It was a compliment, and I'm keeping it."

On the way home, Eli fell asleep in the car. That evening he played his multiplayer game as usual, but through his door I heard him telling his friends about the cave and the colony of swallows. Then he came out and asked me, "Uh, Dad, when can we go again?"

Questions:
What does Eli like to do on a Saturday?
He likes to play multiplayer games in his room with friends.
What did the father tell Eli about Pennsylvania?
He told him that Pennsylvania is officially a commonwealth, not a state.
Why did Eli say, "This is torture"?
He said it because his boat turned in circles and his arms were tired.
What did they find in the rock by the river?
They found a low, dark cave with a colony of swallows.
Why did the father not take offense at Eli's words?
He did not take offense because Eli meant his words as a compliment.
What did Eli ask at the end of the day?
He asked when they could go again.

lessons.title: A Weekend in the Hills
lessons.summary: In an email to a friend, Nadia describes a free weekend workshop where she learned basic skills for nature trips.
lessons.text:
Hi Rosa,

You asked me about the weekend workshop, so here is the whole story. I hope it persuades you to come to the next one with me.

The workshop was held at a camp in the hills, about an hour from the city. It was a residential workshop, which means that we all stayed there for two nights in wooden cabins. I was nervous about that at first, but sharing a cabin with three strangers turned out to be one of the best parts. By Sunday, they no longer felt like strangers at all.

The group that runs the workshop is called Trails for All. It wants people from every ethnic background to feel at home in nature. On the first evening, their leader, Denise Johnson, told us that in many families in this country, from many different ethnic groups, nobody ever went camping, so the children never had a chance to acquire the basic skills. "You don't need expensive equipment," she said. "You need knowledge, and knowledge is free."

After dinner, Denise gave each of us a printed agenda. The agenda was clear and simple: Saturday morning, maps and finding your way; Saturday afternoon, first aid; Sunday morning, cooking and clean water; Sunday afternoon, a short hike to practice everything together. At the start of each session, the teacher would outline the main ideas on a large sheet of paper. Once the main points were outlined, we went outside and tried them ourselves.

I should mention that participation was never an obligation. If someone was tired, or did not feel ready to try something, they could simply watch. Denise believes that people learn better when they feel free, and I think she is right. In fact, participation was almost one hundred percent, because the sessions were so much fun.

In just two days, I managed to acquire skills that I had always thought were too hard for me. I can now read a map with a compass, clean a small wound and make stream water safe to drink. I had always believed that acquiring such skills would take months, so I was very pleased with myself.

The best news is that there is an upcoming workshop at the same camp in June, and there are still places. There is no obligation to pay; they only ask for a small donation from people who can afford it. I have already put the date of the upcoming workshop in my calendar, and I will send you all the details tomorrow. Please say yes!

Love,
Nadia

Questions:
Why was it called a residential workshop?
It was called a residential workshop because everyone stayed at the camp for two nights.
What does the group Trails for All want?
It wants people from every ethnic background to feel at home in nature.
What was on the agenda for Saturday?
Maps and finding your way were on the agenda in the morning, and first aid in the afternoon.
What did the teacher do at the start of each session?
The teacher would outline the main ideas on a large sheet of paper.
Was participation an obligation?
No, participation was never an obligation, but almost everyone took part.
When is the upcoming workshop?
The upcoming workshop is in June.

lessons.title: The Trout of Silver Creek
lessons.summary: A short report on how farmers, fishermen and scientists worked together to save the native trout of a mountain creek.
lessons.text:
Ten years ago, Silver Creek in western Montana was in trouble. For generations, the creek had been famous for its native trout, a beautiful fish with red marks under its chin. By 2015, however, scientists counted fewer than 200 adult native trout in the whole creek.

There were two main problems. The first was water consumption. Silver Creek flows through a wide agricultural valley, and in dry summers the farms took so much water for their fields that some parts of the creek almost disappeared. Nobody was doing anything wrong; water consumption had simply grown together with the farms.

The second problem was genetic. Many years ago, people had put rainbow trout from other states into the creek, and these fish had mixed with the native ones. As a result, the native fish were losing the genetic features that helped them survive in cold mountain water. Scientists warned that the original genetic line could disappear within twenty years.

In 2016, a group of farmers, fishermen and scientists created a new entity, the Silver Creek Trust, to manage a conservation plan. The trust is an independent entity: it is not part of the state government, but it works closely with it.

The hardest part of the plan was the negotiation with the farmers. The trust could not simply tell agricultural families to use less water, because their income depended on it. Instead, it had to negotiate. The negotiation took almost two years. In the end, the farmers agreed to take less water during the driest weeks of summer, and in return they receive compensation for the crops they lose. The money for this compensation comes from the state, from private donors and from fishing licenses.

Most farmers say that the process was fair. "They didn't come here to blame us," one farmer said. "They came to negotiate, and they listened."

The implementation of the plan began in 2018. Workers removed many of the rainbow trout, built small pools where young native fish could grow, and planted trees along the banks to keep the water cool. The implementation has not always been easy, and the work is far from finished. Nevertheless, last year scientists counted more than 1,500 adult native trout in Silver Creek. For a conservation project, that is a remarkable result, and it shows that conservation works best when everyone has a voice.

Questions:
What was the first problem in Silver Creek?
The first problem was water consumption, because the farms took so much water that parts of the creek almost disappeared.
Why was the second problem called genetic?
It was called genetic because rainbow trout had mixed with the native fish, and the native fish were losing their original features.
What is the Silver Creek Trust?
It is an independent entity that manages the conservation plan.
Why did the trust have to negotiate with the farmers?
It had to negotiate because the farmers' income depended on the water.
What do the farmers receive in return for using less water?
They receive compensation for the crops they lose.
What happened after the implementation of the plan?
The number of adult native trout grew from fewer than 200 to more than 1,500.

lessons.title: Wet Socks and Other Pleasures
lessons.summary: A columnist reflects on a rainy camping weekend and why bad weather can be a gift.
lessons.text:
Wet Socks and Other Pleasures
By Helen Brooks

Everyone loves a camping trip in perfect weather. Blue skies, warm afternoons, a clear night full of stars: these are the pictures we see in magazines and on the walls of outdoor shops. Today, I would like to say a few words for the other kind of trip, the one where it rains.

Last month my husband and I drove to a lake in the mountains for the weekend. On Saturday morning the sky was clear. By noon, however, the weather was changing rapidly. Dark clouds came over the mountains, the wind grew cold, and the temperature fell rapidly. Within twenty minutes we were walking through steady rain. We had no clue it was coming, because the forecast had promised sunshine.

By the time we reached our tent, our boots were full of water, and so were our socks. There is a special kind of misery in wet socks. Yet there is also a special joy in taking them off, drying your feet and putting on a dry pair that you have kept at the bottom of your bag for exactly this moment. Every experienced walker will tell you the same thing: you ought to carry one more pair of socks than you think you need.

We spent the afternoon inside the tent, listening to the rain on the roof. We played cards. We read. We ate the bag of candy that was meant for the next day, one piece at a time, as if each candy were a small prize. My husband fell asleep for an hour.

I am not a great defender of bad weather. If you asked me to choose, I would choose sunshine every time. Still, I have become a defender of the rainy day in a tent, because it forces us to slow down. Our modern lifestyle fills every empty moment with screens, messages and plans. A rainy afternoon in a tent cannot be filled that way. It gives you nothing to do, and that is exactly its gift.

I have no clue whether it will rain on our next trip. But I know what I will pack: a deck of cards, a good book, a bag of candy and three dry pairs of socks. Perhaps that is the real lesson. An outdoor lifestyle does not mean always being comfortable. It means being ready to enjoy whatever the sky decides to bring. Anyone who loves the outdoors ought to try a rainy weekend at least once.

Questions:
How did the weather change on Saturday?
By noon the weather was changing rapidly, and soon it was raining.
Why were Helen and her husband surprised by the rain?
They had no clue it was coming, because the forecast had promised sunshine.
What advice does every experienced walker give?
You ought to carry one more pair of socks than you think you need.
How did they eat the candy?
They ate it one piece at a time, as if each candy were a small prize.
Why has Helen become a defender of the rainy day?
She has become a defender of it because it forces people to slow down.
What does an outdoor lifestyle mean, in Helen's opinion?
It means being ready to enjoy whatever the sky decides to bring.

lessons.title: Sunrise on Bear Peak
lessons.summary: Ana climbs to the top of a mountain in the dark to watch the sunrise and meets a man who has come every year for thirty years.
lessons.text:
Ana's alarm rang at 3:30 in the morning. For a moment, she did not know where she was. Then she heard the wind against her tent and remembered: she was camping just below the top of Bear Peak, and she wanted to see the sun come up. She was awake at once, more awake than she ever felt on a work day.

She put on every warm layer she had and started up the last part of the trail with a small lamp on her head. The path was steep but clear, and the stars above her were brighter than she had ever seen them. After 40 minutes she reached the top. Three other people were already there, sitting quietly on the rocks.

One of them was an old man in a red hat. He introduced himself as Walter and told Ana that he was a retired scholar who had spent 40 years studying old maps of the West. He had climbed Bear Peak for a sunrise every September for 30 years. "Scholars spend too much time indoors," he said. "This is my cure."

Slowly, the sky in the east began to change. First it turned a deep purple, then a softer purple with a thin line of pink beneath it. The valleys below were still dark, and long white clouds lay suspended above them, as if they were resting on nothing. "Gorgeous," a young woman next to them said softly. It really was gorgeous, and it was only the beginning.

Then, in an instant, the edge of the sun appeared above the far mountains. Light poured over the land in an explosion of gold and orange. The purple was gone, the suspended clouds turned white, and every rock on the peak seemed to shine. For an instant, nobody moved or spoke. Like millions of other viewers, Ana had seen sunrises in photos and films, but no screen had prepared her for the real light on her face.

When the sun was fully up, the small group of viewers began to talk again. Walter said that the explosion of light was always his favorite moment. Then he took a small notebook out of his pocket and wrote a short paragraph. He told Ana that he wrote one paragraph after every sunrise on the peak, so the notebook now held 30 paragraphs about the same view. "And no two are the same," he said.

Ana walked back down in the bright morning, wide awake and happy. That evening at home, she opened a notebook of her own and wrote her first paragraph about the sunrise on Bear Peak.

Questions:
Why did Ana get up at 3:30 in the morning?
She wanted to see the sun come up from the top of Bear Peak.
Who was Walter?
He was a retired scholar who had studied old maps of the West.
What color did the sky turn first?
It turned a deep purple.
What did the clouds look like?
They lay suspended above the valleys, as if they were resting on nothing.
What happened when the sun appeared?
In an instant, light poured over the land in an explosion of gold and orange.
What does Walter write after every sunrise?
He writes a short paragraph in his notebook.
